claims.text: Cold-spray deposition of CoCrFeNiMo0.85 can repair or improve damaged high-value steel or Ni-based alloy component surfaces.
The cold-spray intervention will form a dense, fine-grained surface layer.
The deposited layer will have minimal interfacial porosity and sound metallurgical bonding to the damaged substrate.
The cold-sprayed coating will significantly increase surface hardness relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed coating will reduce wear rates relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
The cold-sprayed coating will improve corrosion resistance relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
Under aggressive service conditions, the intervention will significantly delay or prevent hot-crack initiation relative to fusion-welded and untreated surfaces.
Cleaning, surface roughening, and optimized spray parameters can produce robust metallurgical bonding.
The proposed process uses a substrate preheated to approximately 150 °C and an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation.
Particle velocities of 600–800 m/s are appropriate for the proposed coating process.
Rapid particle impacts during cold spraying induce severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear.
Impact-induced severe plastic deformation and adiabatic shear cause dynamic grain refinement.
Cold spraying forms the repair layer without melting the base material.
Avoiding base-material melting preserves substrate integrity relative to fusion-welding repair.
The dense, refined, well-bonded layer mechanically protects the surface and resists crack initiation.
The intervention is expected to be effective when damage is primarily superficial.
Severe subsurface damage may require alternative or additional repair methods.
Performance is sensitive to interfacial quality and control of processing parameters.
Long-term durability under cyclic thermal and mechanical loading remains unvalidated.

contradictions.description: The process is described as being conducted at room temperature while the substrate is simultaneously specified as preheated to approximately 150 °C. This is internally ambiguous unless 'room temperature' refers only to the surrounding environment or to the absence of bulk melting.
